# From curves to function fields

Algebraic-geometry (AG) codes replace the polynomial evaluation space of Reed--Solomon codes by a Riemann--Roch space on a curve. The central benefit is that a curve over a finite field can have many rational points relative to its genus, providing long evaluation codes with controlled rate and distance [@goppa1983algebraico; @stichtenoth2009algebraic].

::: {#def-ag-function-field .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: algebraic function field

An algebraic function field $F/\mathbb F_q$ in one variable is a finite extension of $\mathbb F_q(x)$ for some element $x$ transcendental over $\mathbb F_q$. We assume that $\mathbb F_q$ is the full constant field of $F$: every element of $F$ algebraic over $\mathbb F_q$ already lies in $\mathbb F_q$.
:::

For a smooth projective geometrically irreducible curve $X/\mathbb F_q$, its rational-function field $\mathbb F_q(X)$ is such a function field. Conversely, one-variable function fields correspond to smooth projective curves up to the appropriate notion of isomorphism. Passing to the smooth projective model removes artifacts of a particular affine equation and includes points at infinity.

## Elliptic-curve example

Assume $\operatorname{char}\mathbb F_q\ne2,3$ and

$$
E:y^2=x^3+ax+b,
\qquad 4a^3+27b^2\ne0.
$$

Then

$$
\mathbb F_q(E)=\mathbb F_q(x,y),
\qquad y^2=x^3+ax+b,
$$

is a degree-two extension of $\mathbb F_q(x)$. Every element can be written

$$
f(x)+y,g(x),
\qquad f,g\in\mathbb F_q(x),
$$

because every power $y^j$ reduces to degree at most one in $y$.

# Places and valuations

The phrase “evaluate a rational function at a point” is made intrinsic through places.

::: {#def-ag-place .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: place and valuation ring

A place $P$ of $F/\mathbb F_q$ is represented by a discrete valuation ring

$$
\mathbb F_q\subseteq\mathcal O_P\subsetneq F
$$

with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_P$. Its residue field and degree are

$$
F_P=\mathcal O_P/\mathfrak m_P,
\qquad
\deg P=[F_P:\mathbb F_q].
$$

There is a normalized discrete valuation

$$
v_P:F^\times\longrightarrow\mathbb Z
$$

such that $\mathcal O_P=\{f:v_P(f)\ge0\}$ and $\mathfrak m_P=\{f:v_P(f)>0\}$.
:::

For $f,g\in F^\times$,

$$
v_P(fg)=v_P(f)+v_P(g),
\qquad
v_P(f+g)\ge\min\{v_P(f),v_P(g)\}.
$$

If the two valuations in the minimum are unequal, equality holds. Positive valuation means a zero, negative valuation a pole, and valuation zero a local unit.

## Rational-function-field example

For $F=\mathbb F_q(x)$, every monic irreducible polynomial $p(x)$ defines a finite place $P_p$ with

$$
v_{P_p}\!\left(\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}\right)
=\operatorname{ord}_p a-\operatorname{ord}_p b,
\qquad
\deg P_p=\deg p.
$$

There is also a place at infinity,

$$
v_{P_\infty}\!\left(\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}\right)
=\deg b-\deg a.
$$

Degree-one places correspond to $x=\alpha$ for $\alpha\in\mathbb F_q$, together with $P_\infty$.

# Divisors

::: {#def-ag-divisor .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: divisor

A divisor is a finite formal sum

$$
D=\sum_P n_PP,
\qquad n_P\in\mathbb Z.
$$

Its support and degree are

$$
\operatorname{supp}D=\{P:n_P\ne0\},
\qquad
\deg D=\sum_Pn_P\deg P.
$$
:::

For $f\in F^\times$, the principal divisor is

$$
(f)=\sum_Pv_P(f)P=(f)_0-(f)_\infty,
$$

where

$$
(f)_0=\sum_{v_P(f)>0}v_P(f)P,
\qquad
(f)_\infty=\sum_{v_P(f)<0}-v_P(f)P.
$$

Every principal divisor has degree zero. Divisors modulo principal divisors form the divisor class group.

::: {#def-ag-riemann-roch-space .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: Riemann--Roch space

For a divisor $G$, define

$$
\mathcal L(G)=\{0\}\cup
\{f\in F^\times:(f)+G\ge0\},
\qquad
\ell(G)=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\mathcal L(G).
$$

Thus $G$ bounds the allowed poles of $f$.
:::

For $F=\mathbb F_q(x)$,

$$
\mathcal L(mP_\infty)
=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_q}\{1,x,\ldots,x^m\}
$$

when $m\ge0$.

# Riemann--Roch theorem

::: {#thm-ag-riemann-roch .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem: Riemann--Roch

Let $F/\mathbb F_q$ have genus $g$, and let $K$ be a canonical divisor. For every divisor $G$,

$$
\ell(G)-\ell(K-G)=\deg G+1-g.
$$
:::

Two immediate consequences are

$$
\deg G<0\Longrightarrow\ell(G)=0
$$

and

$$
\deg G>2g-2\Longrightarrow\ell(G)=\deg G+1-g.
$$

The first implication is not an equivalence: a divisor of nonnegative degree can still have $\ell(G)=0$.

# Evaluation codes

Choose distinct rational places $P_1,\ldots,P_n$ and let

$$
D=P_1+\cdots+P_n.
$$

Choose a divisor $G$ with $\operatorname{supp}G\cap\operatorname{supp}D=\varnothing$.

::: {#def-ag-evaluation-code .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: functional AG code

The functional AG code is

$$
C_L(D,G)=
\{(f(P_1),\ldots,f(P_n)):f\in\mathcal L(G)\}
\subseteq\mathbb F_q^n.
$$
:::

::: {#thm-ag-code-parameters .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem: designed parameters

If $\deg G<n$, then evaluation is injective and $C_L(D,G)$ has parameters

$$
k=\ell(G),
\qquad
d\ge n-\deg G.
$$

If additionally $2g-2<\deg G<n$, then

$$
k=\deg G+1-g.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

If a nonzero $f\in\mathcal L(G)$ vanishes at all $P_i$, then

$$
(f)+G-D\ge0.
$$

Taking degrees gives $0+\deg G-n\ge0$, contradicting $\deg G<n$. Hence evaluation is injective and $k=\ell(G)$.

If a nonzero codeword has zeros at $t$ evaluation places, then $(f)+G$ contains those $t$ places, so $t\le\deg G$. Therefore its weight is at least $n-\deg G$. The dimension formula in the nonspecial range follows from Riemann--Roch.
:::

# Reed--Solomon codes as genus-zero AG codes

Take $F=\mathbb F_q(x)$, $G=mP_\infty$, and $D=P_{\alpha_1}+\cdots+P_{\alpha_n}$ for distinct $\alpha_i\in\mathbb F_q$. Then

$$
C_L(D,mP_\infty)
=\{(f(\alpha_1),\ldots,f(\alpha_n)):\deg f\le m\}.
$$

It has

$$
[n,k,d]=[n,m+1,n-m],
$$

which meets the Singleton bound. AG codes generalize this construction by allowing positive genus and, crucially, curves with more rational evaluation points than the projective line.

# Hermitian-curve example

Over $\mathbb F_{q^2}$, the Hermitian curve

$$
y^q+y=x^{q+1}
$$

has genus $g=q(q-1)/2$ and $q^3+1$ rational places. For every $\alpha\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$, the trace equation

$$
y^q+y=\alpha^{q+1}\in\mathbb F_q
$$

has $q$ solutions in $\mathbb F_{q^2}$, producing $q^3$ affine rational points; the projective closure contributes one point at infinity. One-point divisors $G=mP_\infty$ therefore yield long, structured evaluation codes.

# From classical AG codes to quantum codes

Nested classical codes can be converted into CSS codes. If

$$
C_Z^\perp\subseteq C_X\subseteq\mathbb F_q^n,
$$

then the associated CSS code has dimension

$$
k_Q=\dim C_X+\dim C_Z-n
$$

and distances controlled by vectors outside the relevant dual subcodes. Suitable nested AG evaluation and differential codes provide asymptotically good quantum codes [@ashikhmin2001asymptotically]. The nontrivial work is not merely choosing two divisors: one must verify the duality relation, field assumptions, and the resulting quantum distances.

The homological construction in [Homological and Hyperbolic Surface Codes](homological-and-hyperbolic-codes.qmd) uses chain complexes rather than function fields, but both approaches organize CSS orthogonality through paired algebraic spaces.
